F1:
The operating reserve is the one part of Laura's plan where we left no room for opinion. The case wants 10 payments of $50,000 from 2033 to 2042 met with 'a high degree of certainty' from the portfolio alone, so the reserve is all Treasuries, all bought by January 2028: the 10 in January 2027, for about $302,000, then the first $38,282 of the 2028 deposit – $2,388 to finish the 10 (the top-up), and $35,894 on extra Treasuries.

At first glance that last figure looks like paying for the same payments twice. It isn't. A Treasury pays what it says, but on its own date, and Laura pays on 1 January – the February 2037 bond ends ten and a half months before the 2038 payment it funds, and coupons arrive all along the way. Whatever that waiting money earns is the one part of the payments no Treasury locks in. Without the extra Treasuries, the 10 need it to earn about 5.1% a year; tested on every starting month since 1962, all 585 of them, the 10 alone would have fallen short in about 56 of every 100, and by about $34,500 in a bad 1-in-20 case. Roughly a coin toss – hardly 'a high degree of certainty'.

So we used the escrow agent's test, 'sufficient without reinvestment': the 10 are paid in full even if every coupon and every dollar of waiting cash earns nothing at all. It asks more than the case does, on purpose – it means the payments need nothing from future interest rates.

And most of that price comes back. By 1 January 2033 the reserve is worth about $444,500, about 111% of what the 10 are worth that day; if rates simply do what the market expects, about $45,500 (in 2033 money) is left over and comes back to Laura, about $74,100 by 2042 if it sits in a Treasury-bill fund. The payments rest on Treasuries alone, and on nothing that has to earn a cent.

The IPS gives only 2 reasons to change the plan – a missed deposit or a Treasury default – and both are defined tightly, because a loose trigger is just permission to fiddle. A missed deposit means nothing received by 31 March 2028; anything that does arrive is simply a smaller deposit, run in the same order as a full one. If nothing came, no range is stated in 2031 and the 2033 payment is about $3,000 short at today's rates. A Treasury default means a Treasury payment more than five business days late. Those are the only 2 events that reach what the payments rest on – the money to buy the Treasuries, and the Treasuries paying.

Everything else is a watch: checked and logged, and at most a swap of one Treasury holding for another. If an end moves past the payment it funds, it's swapped for a Treasury maturing first, any cost paid from the extra Treasuries, never the shares. Market prices? Carry on. A fall in yields matters to the bottom of the range only until January 2028, and to the top only until the 2031 move, so the top isn't said aloud until then. C1: We know Treasury bonds (including this one – maturing 2037) won't create wealth, but they will remove uncertainty, through duration-matching. In other words, we take Laura's requested 'high degree of certainty' to mean a near-ironclad guarantee, and we provide exactly that. Every year the bonds sit untouched is a good year – one less year of Laura's money being exposed to anything the restless markets might decide to do. Notably – Laura's payments are fixed in nominal dollars, so a nominal Treasury matches the liability perfectly, meaning we don't need TIPS, which would hedge against a nonexistent inflation risk.
C2: Some years, WInS lists no Treasuries maturing – so we purchased iShares iBonds (like IBTM for 2032) instead. Defined-maturity, investment-grade, liquid, cheap and transparent about yields, these behave a lot like bonds when held to their end – so we'll simply ignore price noise in the interim. Together, our T-Bonds and iBonds ensure each of Laura's payments rests on a dedicated instrument (not merely a forecast). The catch is, their terminal payout is a net asset value, as opposed to a promise of par – but in return we gain a level of liquidity which no odd-lot bond offers.
C3: VT is where we allow ourselves to be wrong – because it's the only investment not standing between Laura and a payment deadline. This ETF owns thousands of companies, diversified across countries and sectors, which means we can avoid paying the price for the vain illusion that we can pick winners, instead buying the entire market's growth premium at an expense ratio of just 0.06%, for a forecast return of about 7.5% a year (as per JPMorgan). The T-Bonds and iBonds already cover the operating commitments, so VT answers a different question – how generous can the facility contribution be?
X1: Pension funds cover fixed payments either by matching their bonds' average life to the payments and rebalancing as rates move, or by buying one bond per payment and holding it. We do the second, which needs no forecast or trading. In January 2027, her first $300,000 buys a ladder of Treasury bonds and Treasury funds with fixed end dates, each maturing just before a January payment. A Treasury held to maturity pays exactly what it promised, whatever markets do, so no payment depends on shares.
X2:
In 2031, Laura gives co-sponsors a range. The bottom is the floor, rounded down: money she already owns. The top adds half her shares, which move into Treasuries before she names it, because a number said aloud can't quietly be halved after a bad year. The other half stays hers and liquid, as a cushion if the building costs more in Taiwan dollars.

The ladder's one weakness is that it counts on reinvesting its bonds' interest; if rates fall and stay low, it can fall short. Before Laura names her range, we price that shortfall at the day's rates, add a margin, and move that much from her kept shares into Treasuries. Her spare money shrinks before her promise does, and if it can't cover the gap, the whole range comes down.
